reason: The sources corroborate 20 distinct claims detailing New Horizons' record launch velocity, ALMA navigation, and Pluto flyby carrying earthly mementos.
story: In 1991, the U.S. Postal Service released stamps celebrating planetary exploration. Every world showed a spacecraft, except the ninth, which bore a stinging challenge: 'Pluto: Not Yet Explored.' Rankled scientists used that stamp as a battle cry to make a mission happen. On January 19, 2006, NASA launched New Horizons directly into a solar escape trajectory at an Earth-relative speed of 16.26 kilometers per second, making it the fastest human-made object ever launched from Earth. To ensure the probe hit its mark across three billion miles, astronomers used the ALMA radio telescope array in Chile to precisely calculate Pluto's orbit. After a speed boost from Jupiter and a nine-and-a-half-year journey, New Horizons sped past Pluto on July 14, 2015, traveling at over 52,000 miles per hour. Tucked inside were nine cultural mementos, including that very 1991 'Not Yet Explored' stamp, finally delivered to the edge of the solar system.
angle: NASA launched the fastest probe in history to Pluto carrying the 1991 'Not Yet Explored' postage stamp that originally provoked scientists into building the mission.

claims.claim: New Horizons launched from Earth on January 19, 2006.
New Horizons was launched directly into an escape trajectory to exit the Solar System.
The probe achieved an Earth-relative launch velocity of 16.26 kilometers per second (approximately 36,000 mph).
New Horizons was the fastest human-made object ever launched from Earth.
In 2007, New Horizons executed a flyby of Jupiter to receive a gravity assist.
The Jupiter gravity assist increased the probe's speed by approximately 4 kilometers per second.
Pluto was originally discovered in 1930.
Astronomers used the ALMA radio telescope array in Chile to measure Pluto's position and orbit to help guide New Horizons.
Alan Stern served as the principal investigator for the New Horizons mission.
Alan Stern is affiliated with the Southwest Research Institute.
Robert Staehle helped originate Pluto mission concepts that led up to New Horizons, including the Pluto 350 study.
New Horizons carries nine cultural mementos in its cargo.
The probe carries a 1991 U.S. postage stamp bearing the phrase 'Pluto: Not Yet Explored'.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
The voyage to Pluto took approximately 9.5 years to complete.
New Horizons flew past Pluto on July 14, 2015.
New Horizons was the first spacecraft to fly by and study Pluto up close.
New Horizons reached speeds topping 52,000 mph (84,000 km/h) during its mission.
It took roughly 16 months for New Horizons to transmit all its Pluto encounter data back to Earth.
Following its Pluto flyby, New Horizons continued into the Kuiper Belt and visited the object Arrokoth.

disputed: Clyde Tombaugh's ashes: Wikipedia [S1] states that about 30 grams of Pluto discoverer Clyde Tombaugh's ashes are aboard New Horizons, but no other provided source mentions this detail. Under the two-site rule, the script should leave out the ashes claim.

Record speed distinctions: New Horizons set the record for the fastest launch velocity from Earth, but probes falling toward the Sun (such as Helios and Parker Solar Probe) achieved higher heliocentric or orbital speeds. The script should explicitly clarify it was the fastest object launched from Earth.

Pluto's planetary classification: While the IAU reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006, New Horizons team members like Alan Stern dispute the IAU definition and continue to advocate for Pluto as a planet; attribute this debate to mission scientists.
